newsitem.title: USA: Local job growth seen slower in 1997 -- Phila. Fed.
newsitem.headline: Local job growth seen slower in 1997 -- Phila. Fed.

text.p: Overall growth and job creation in the third U.S. economic district is expected to be somewhat slower in 1997 than it was last year, a Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia economist said.

"For 1997, we look for somewhat slower growth than we had last year ... We're looking for slightly slower job growth in all three states in 1997," Ted Crone, vice president and an economist at the Philadelphia Fed, told Reuters.
The Philadelphia Fed serves the nation's third economic district, which encompasses Delaware, the eastern region of Pennsylvania and the southern portion of New Jersey.
Crone said expectations for slower job growth in 1997 follow a strong pace of job creation in 1996.
"We are not going to be rebounding from a weak year ... Though we had momentum going into 1997, we don't expect the job growth (in 1997) to actually match what we had last year," Crone said.
The Philadelphia Fed economist said, however, he expected the unemployment rate in the region to dip a little before it comes back up slightly.
"We do expect the unemployment rates to dip down a little bit, at least in New Jersey and Delaware through the year, and initially drop in Pennsylvania before they come back up a little," Crone said.
Crone said the labor markets in the region are tight. He added, however, the firmness in the employment sector tends to be concentrated in some labor categories and specific areas.
"We have some tightening in the labor markets, but it tends to be spotty," Crone said, adding that strong demand for workers was more concentrated on skilled categories.
The Philadelphia Fed economist also said he has seen some wage pressures in the region, but they were also concentrated in some specific areas.
"We are seeing some wage pressures, but it's spotty; it's by occupation. The wage pressures here are certainly not as great as they are in other parts of the country," Crone said.
Crone said consumer spending in the region appeared to be faring well.
"They (consumers) seem to be holding up fairly well," the Philadelphia Fed economist said.

"I think our biggest increase at least in sales in Pennsylvania and New Jersey actually was in the first half of last year. But it isn't that people have backtracked. They held up pretty well," Crone added.
The Philadelphia Fed is one of the 12 regional banks in the Federal Reserve System.

The Philadephia Fed is headed by Edward Boehne, a member of the central bank's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). Boehne is not scheduled to vote on FOMC policy actions in 1997 given the committee's rotation rules.

The Federal Reserve last changed short-term interest rates on March 25, when the central bank raised its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent during the last meeting of its policy-setting body.
